dedupe_keys.name: oroville dam spillway incident independent forensic team review california 2017

description: This case study is the forensic review of the February 2017 Oroville Dam spillway incident in California. After the incident the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission required the California Department of Water Resources (DWR), owner of the dam and of the State Water Project that supplies about 25 million people and 750,000 acres of irrigated farmland, to engage an Independent Forensic Team; ASDSO and the United States Society on Dams recommended its six members. The team released preliminary findings in May 2017, an interim memorandum in September 2017 and its final report on 5 January 2018. It covers one site, from design and construction in the 1960s to the incident, and describes how uplift of the service spillway chute slab on 7 February 2017 exposed poor foundation rock to erosion, how later decisions let the emergency spillway overtop for the first time, and how headcutting erosion led to an evacuation order for about 188,000 downstream residents on 12 February. Evidence included design and geology records, inspections, failure mode analyses, operation records, Incident Command notes, more than 75 interviews and staff surveys. The report is a free PDF of about 580 pages hosted by ASDSO and mirrored at Stanford's National Performance of Dams Program; no licence is stated. Caveats: it gives causes and lessons, not a hydraulic or risk model, and assigns no individual blame. Simulation uses: a reference post-event case for dam failure modes, spillway erosion, cascading operational risks (spillway, powerhouse, transmission) and evacuation planning. Related records: the worldwide dam failures database (data-worldwide-historical-dam-failures-database), the US National Inventory of Dams (data-usace-national-inventory-of-dams) and HEC-RAS (model-hec-ras).

outcomes: The team found no single root cause: chute slab uplift from water injection through cracks and joints, poor foundation rock and deteriorated repairs, compounded by decisions that let the untested emergency spillway overtop, led to the order evacuating about 188,000 people; it attributed the incident to long-term systemic failure of DWR, regulatory and industry practice and set out industry lessons.
